materials.passage:
For six months, a local group in the fictional town of Pineford has been preparing a small gallery in an unused community building. The group wants neighbors to share stories about objects they have made or kept. The gallery is not a shop, and the display will be free to visit. Each exhibit will have a short note explaining who lent it and why it matters to them. Before placing a work in a room, the team asks its owner for permission and checks whether the story in the note is accurate.

The first room contains an image of the river near the town. A local artist named Ada made this image on canvas. Her landscape shows the river in the early morning, before the streets become busy. Ada chose a simple wooden frame, and she has written a note about the changing light. The scene is familiar to many visitors, but Ada hopes they will notice details they usually pass on their way to work. She has painted by the river since she moved to Pineford three years ago.

Across the room is a portrait of an older woman named Rosa. Her grandson made it last winter. The original drawing was much smaller; he later made a larger version for the gallery. Rosa asked him to include the blue scarf she wears when she tells stories to children. The picture is modern in style, but the scarf reminds Rosa of a traditional celebration in her family. The note does not claim that every family in their culture has the same customs.

The next room is devoted to craft, with work from several neighbors. One person has worked with clay for five years and has lent a ceramic bowl. She learned pottery from a neighbor who showed her how to shape the clay. Beside the bowl is a small sculpture of a bird. It is not a statue of a famous person; it is an imagined bird that the maker created after a walk. Another neighbor has added a piece of fabric that she made from old shirts. A guide explains that a textile can carry a memory of the person who used it. The collection is small, but every object has a different story.

The team has already arranged a short tour for Saturday morning. They have not finished the labels yet, so everyone is helping with the final details. The guide will invite visitors to ask questions, but nobody has to share a personal story. At the end of the tour, people can sit at a table and try to create a small drawing of an ordinary thing. Ada says that a creative idea does not need to be expensive or perfect. The group hopes that the gallery will become a place where neighbors listen to one another as well as look at art.

Luis: What about the second room?
Ava: There is a sculpture made from clay and a small ceramic bowl. The person who made them has practiced pottery for four years. The sculpture is an animal, but it is not a statue of a real pet.
Luis: I have already written a note for the bowl, but I have not written the note for the sculpture yet. I will finish it tonight.
Ava: Thank you. We also have a colorful piece of fabric made by a textile group. The group uses an old craft in a modern style. They say each object can tell a story about culture without representing every person in a community.
Luis: Will a guide lead the tour?
Ava: Yes. The guide will speak for twenty minutes and then invite questions. Visitors may create a small drawing at the table, but they do not have to show it to anyone.
Luis: That sounds welcoming. Is the portrait for sale?
Ava: No. This is a free event, and the artist will take it home afterward. I hope people notice how different a familiar scene can look in another person's work.
Luis: I agree. A creative display can help neighbors talk about things they might otherwise pass without noticing.

1. 在 Could you tell me 后引出间接特殊疑问句时，从句使用陈述语序：疑问词 + 主语 + 动词。直接问 Where is the room?，间接问 Could you tell me where the room is? 不重复倒装。

2. 间接一般疑问句可用 if 或 whether 引出，意思是“是否”；后面仍用主语 + 动词，不使用 do / does 倒装。whether 在正式或需要突出选择时也适用。

3. Could you / Would you mind 用于提出礼貌请求；mind 后接动词 ing。句末标点取决于整句话：直接请求疑问句用问号，I wonder if 引导的陈述句通常用句号。

materials.instructions: Read the passage and choose one answer for each question.
materials.passage:
Sofia and Ben are preparing a small discussion evening at a community center. On Monday, Sofia sends Ben a message: “We need the room on Thursday.” The sentence gives a day, but it does not give a time. Ben assumes that the event is in the morning, because another group usually meets there then. Sofia thinks he knows that she means five in the afternoon. Neither person has checked the other's idea.

On Tuesday, Ben sees that the room is already booked in the morning. His first response is to write “This is urgent!” in a message to Sofia. He wants to explain the problem quickly, but he does not mention the morning booking. Sofia reads the word “urgent” and feels upset because she thinks the whole event must be canceled. She waits until she has a quiet moment to reply. Instead of guessing again, she suggests a short conversation after lunch.

When they meet, Sofia asks Ben to describe what he found. She tries to listen without interrupting. Ben says that he was looking at the morning booking. Sofia explains that her plan is for five in the afternoon. “I should have included the time,” she says. “I apologize for the confusion.” Ben also apologizes because his message did not say which booking worried him. They agree to check the room schedule together. To clarify the plan, Sofia asks whether Ben can suggest another time if five is unavailable. They will discuss a backup with the manager rather than change the event without asking the group. Their aim is to keep all participants informed.

The room is free after four, so they can use it at five. Ben offers to send a polite request to the center manager. He wants to communicate both the day and the time. Sofia suggests a phrase: “Could you tell me whether the room is available at five on Thursday?” Ben likes the purpose of the question: it asks for confirmation without assuming the manager has made a mistake. They decide not to make the message more formal than necessary, because they know the manager well.

Before sending it, Ben reads the message aloud. Sofia notices that the tone sounds calm. She asks him to repeat the time once, and they compare it with the booking page. The manager later confirms that the room is available. In her opinion, the extra detail is helpful, and she asks them to remind her on Wednesday. Ben and Sofia write a short note after the exchange: if a message seems unclear, ask a question before deciding what the other person meant. Their dialogue does not mean that every misunderstanding has one simple reason, but this time a clear choice of words helped.

materials.transcript:
Iris: I saw your message about the community conversation on Saturday. Did you mean ten in the morning?
Paul: I meant two in the afternoon. I should have written the time clearly. I apologize for the confusion.
Iris: Thanks for explaining. The poster says “Saturday” but does not mention a time. We should clarify it before we print more copies.
Paul: I agree. Could you tell me whether the hall is free at two? I have not received a response from the manager yet.
Iris: I can ask her now. Our purpose is to make sure people have the right information, not to blame anyone.
Paul: Good. The dialogue will be informal, and everyone can share an opinion about neighborhood activities.
Iris: The manager says the hall is free at two. She asks us to remind her on Friday.
Paul: I will reply to her message. Could you repeat which door people should use?
Iris: The side door. The main door is being repaired. Please describe that on the poster in one short sentence.
Paul: How about the phrase “Please enter through the side door”?
Iris: That sounds polite and easy to understand. We can also include a phone number for questions.
Iris: I suggest we explain the reason for the change in a short, clear message, rather than a formal letter.
Paul: Is the change urgent? I do not want our tone to make people upset.
Iris: We have three days, so it is not an emergency. We should still update the poster today.
Paul: I will listen to your suggestion and check the time once more. Then I will send you the final version.
Iris: Thank you. This exchange has helped us communicate the plan clearly. After people arrive, we can discuss their ideas for the next event.

1. somebody / someone 指某个人；anybody / anyone 常用于疑问或否定句。它们作主语时通常接单数动词。语境决定所指，不要仅凭肯定或否定机械判断。

3. it 常指前文的单数事物，they / them 常指复数人或事物；this / that 可指前面提到的情况。若一个代词可能指两个对象，要重写名称消除歧义。

materials.passage:
On a Saturday morning, Lina and her friend Tariq help plan a short community walk in the fictional town of Glenford. They want everyone to understand the route before setting off, including visitors who have never been there. The group will meet beside the library at nine. Someone from the walking club will bring a paper map, and Lina will bring a compass. Neither item replaces local signs or advice; the group will ask the park staff if anything is unclear.

From the library, people should use the sidewalk along the main street until they reach the first junction. The sidewalk is the space for people on foot; the dark pavement beside it is the paved surface used by vehicles. At the intersection, a clock on a tall building is an easy landmark. The guide asks everyone to wait there and check that the whole group has arrived. The club also plans a short rest for anyone who needs one. From the clock they will go east toward a bridge over a stream. They will not enter the old tunnel nearby because the park has closed it for maintenance.

Beyond the bridge is a field with a low fence. A broad path follows the water for a while and then turns south into a meadow. In spring the meadow has flowers, and the group can stop without leaving the marked trail. Tariq points to a hill on the west side of the valley. Its lower slope is gentle, but the upper part is steep and can be slippery after rain. Lina does not plan to climb the hill; she wants a walk that the whole group has agreed is comfortable.

The guide checks the latest local notice before Saturday. It says that the narrow path beside the stream can become muddy. If that path is closed, the walkers will follow a wider track through the field instead. The notice also shows a covered shelter beside the visitor center. This is the second meeting place, not a place to wait alone. If someone becomes separated, they should contact the guide using the number printed on the group note. Nobody needs to guess a direction or hurry to catch up.

On the practice walk, Tariq asks what the word “it” means in their written directions. In the sentence about the tunnel, it refers to the tunnel, not the bridge. They change another sentence so that the name of the path appears instead of an unclear “this.” At the end of the route they descend a short slope back toward the visitor center. Lina sends everyone the two meeting places and a simple reminder to check the park's current information. The story is a language exercise, so real groups should use their own local guidance.

Mina: What happens at the intersection near the clock?

materials.passage:
On Monday, Mei moves into a small apartment in the fictional town of Brookside. Before unpacking, she and the building manager, Alex, make a maintenance list. Mei notices a damp patch near the kitchen sink. Alex checks the record and explains that a pipe under the sink was inspected last week. A qualified worker will return on Wednesday to find out why the area is still damp. Mei does not try to fix the pipe herself.

The faucet above the sink also drips after it is closed. Mei's friend calls it a tap, the usual British word for a faucet. Alex adds it to the list, together with the drain, which is slow to empty. Mei asks for the visit time in writing because she works from home on Wednesday. Alex says the worker is expected between ten and eleven, but the office will call if the appointment changes.

In the living room, there is a small crack near the top of the wall. The roof was checked after a storm, and Alex has already asked a specialist to look at the new mark. Mei moves a light curtain away from the crack and leaves the carpet where it is. Mei takes a photograph of the crack for the report so that the worker can compare the mark with the photograph later. materials.passage:
Iris and Ken are preparing a short article for a fictional community newsletter. It will describe how neighbors repaired a bench near the town garden. Before publishing, Iris reads the headline: “Three Hundred People Built a New Garden.” The number and the description seem different from the notes she took at the event. Ken agrees that every fact in the headline must agree with the text. They decide to verify the numbers before sending the story.

The first paragraph says thirty neighbors helped clean and repair one bench. A later passage says they also planted two small trees. Iris uses a link to open the club's own event record, which lists thirty names and describes the same work. The source is useful because someone recorded it immediately after the event, but Iris still wants to compare it with a second set of notes. She does not assume that one document is always complete or correct.

Ken checks a picture and its caption. The image shows a painted bench, but the caption says that it was a new building. They can zoom in on the picture or enlarge it on the screen; neither action tells them when it was taken. Iris asks the photographer for the original note. With that evidence, they change the caption to “Neighbors beside the repaired bench.” They also correct the claim about three hundred people, since the available record supports thirty.

The draft includes an advertisement for a local paint shop. The publisher has placed a clear label above it so readers can distinguish it from the article. The publication also has a short quote from a gardener: “We enjoyed working together.” A citation identifies the interview where the words came from. Ken wants to forward the draft to the group, but Iris asks him not to send the photograph yet. The people in it have not all given permission for their images to be shared.

They discuss privacy before posting. The club's rule says they must receive permission before publishing an identifiable picture. They should also ask whether anyone wants a name removed. One person may agree to the picture but prefer not to be named; another might ask for the photograph to stay private. Those possibilities are not proof that either person has already made a request. Iris suggests a version without faces while they wait for replies.

The finished newsletter will include a short note about how they checked the story. Readers can choose to subscribe, print a copy, or leave a comment. An icon opens the reading controls, but it does not tell readers whether a claim is true. Ken says that media can offer helpful information and can also show bias when important details are missing. The result of their check is a smaller, more accurate story. The people and newsletter in this exercise are invented.

materials.passage:
Nia works at a fictional community center. For years, her morning routine began with a rushed bus ride and no breakfast. She used to leave home as soon as she woke up, and she often felt sleepy during the first meeting. Now she prepares a few things the night before. Her aim is not to follow a perfect plan; she wants enough time to notice which habits suit her own schedule. One habit she wants to keep is leaving a little extra time in the morning.

Nia used to go to bed at a different time each night. She now writes down her bedtime and tries to follow a more regular evening routine. If she takes a nap after work, she records when it starts and ends. Her journal is a simple notebook, not a medical test. It helps her ask better questions about her routine, but it cannot prove why she feels a particular way.

At work, Nia used to ignore hunger until the middle of the day. She now packs breakfast and a small snack when she expects a long morning. Her appetite changes from day to day, so she does not force herself to eat the same amount. When she feels thirsty, she takes a drink. She also keeps supper simple on evenings when she returns late. Her friend chooses different foods, and Nia knows that each person has different needs.

At a cooking session, the group reads a short nutrition guide. It explains that a nutrient is a substance in food that helps the body work or grow. The guide names protein, fiber and a vitamin as examples, and says that iron is a mineral. Nia looks at the label on a loaf made with wheat, a type of grain. The guide does not promise that one meal will solve every health problem. The group asks the center for sources so that they can check what the guide says.

Nia also wants to be more active in ways she enjoys. At lunch she walks with a colleague, and she sometimes stops to stretch before returning to her desk. She takes a slow breath and gives herself a quiet minute to relax when work feels busy. She writes about her mood and stress in the notebook without assuming that one activity explains everything. If a muscle hurts or she has a health concern, she plans to ask an appropriate professional rather than guess a treatment.

After three weeks, Nia reads the notes she has made. The changes are gradual: she often leaves home earlier and has more time for breakfast, but some evenings are still busy. She decides to keep the parts of her lifestyle that fit her circumstances and change the plan when necessary. Her colleague likes the idea of recording observations without treating a short diary as proof of a cause. Nia is curious about what she will notice next month.

materials.instructions: Read the passage and choose one answer for each question.
materials.passage:
A volunteer group in the fictional town of Bellmere wants to survey residents about a community room. They invite twenty-five people to answer one question about a possible improvement. Twenty people return the questionnaire, and each participant chooses just one of three options: more seats, a small art display, or more plants. The group calls the twenty responses its sample. A resident who did not answer is not included in those totals.

The record shows that twelve people choose seats, five choose art, and three choose plants. The participation rate is twenty out of twenty-five invited people, or eighty percent. That is different from the percentage choosing seats: twelve out of twenty respondents, or sixty percent. The proportion for plants is three out of twenty, which can be written as the fraction 3/20. The ratio of seat choices to art choices is twelve to five. Every number is labeled so that readers can see which group is being counted.

Twelve is more than half of twenty, so the majority of respondents choose seats. Five is one quarter of twenty and represents the art category. The eight respondents who choose art or plants form a minority of the sample. The group draws a simple chart with three bars: twelve for seats, five for art, and three for plants. The chart does not represent residents who did not reply, and it does not show what every person in town wants.

The group also has a poll from the previous month. It included a different set of twenty respondents: eight chose seats, five chose art, and seven chose plants. In these two small rounds, seat choices increase from eight to twelve. Art choices remain at five, so that count is stable. Plant choices show a decrease from seven to three. A line may rise between the two recorded points, but the group does not call this a long-term trend. Two rounds are not enough to establish one.

To practice another calculation, the group uses three invented waiting times: two, four and nine minutes. Their average, or mean, is five minutes because their sum is fifteen and fifteen divided by three is five. The median is four because it is the middle value when the three times are ordered. These practice numbers are not answers to the room question. The group uses the survey data to estimate how many chairs might be useful for a trial, then asks staff to check the room's capacity.

Before publishing the result, the organizers explain that the sample is small and may not represent the whole town. They invite other residents to comment and plan to ask a wider group next time. The story and numbers are invented for language and arithmetic practice; they are not results from a real community.

materials.instructions: This conversation is fictional. Listen to the conversation before reading the transcript and answer independently. After submitting, check the transcript and reasons for any errors.
materials.transcript:
Omar: We asked twenty residents to answer our questionnaire about the outdoor meeting area. Each participant chose one improvement, and all twenty replied.
Lena: What does the record show?
Omar: Eight chose more seats, six chose shade, and six chose drinking water. The sample is small, so we should not say it represents everyone in town.
Lena: What is the percentage for seats?
Omar: Eight out of twenty is forty percent. The fraction is 8/20, or two fifths. The ratio of seat choices to shade choices is eight to six.
Lena: That means seats are the largest single category, but eight is less than half of twenty. We should not call those eight a majority.
Omar: Exactly. A minority chose seats, even though that option received more votes than either other option. We can put the three counts on a bar chart.
Lena: How does this compare with the earlier poll?
Omar: The earlier poll had another set of twenty people. Four chose seats, eight chose shade, and eight chose water. Seat choices increase from four to eight, while the other two counts show a decrease.
Lena: Can we call that a long-term trend?
Omar: No. There are only two rounds, and the people may be different. We can say that one count may rise or remain stable in a future round, but we cannot know yet.
Lena: What about the average and median in the example on the board?
Omar: Those are practice waiting times, not survey answers. The times are three, five and ten minutes. The mean is six because their sum is eighteen, and eighteen divided by three is six; the median is five because it is the middle number.
Lena: I will write that distinction in our report. We could use the data to estimate what to test next, then ask more residents.
Omar: Good. All twenty invited people replied, so the participation rate was one hundred percent, but it is still only a small group. Let's survey a wider group before making a decision.
